story: What do you get when you cross a symphony orchestra with a star chart? Hopefully, a younger audience.

I started looking at the Colorado Symphony as a constellation: individual musicians and instruments, each with a precise place in the larger composition. Traditional star charts became the jumping-off point, with the orchestra’s stage arrangement translated into a celestial system of points, lines, and patterns.

The visual identity turns the concert hall into something closer to an observatory. Posters, concert collateral, and merchandise map the orchestra into a visual universe—part celestial atlas, part concert identity.
The result is a system that gives the symphony a little more mystery, a little more wonder, and hopefully a reason to look twice.

galen-tines-zine.title: Galen-tines Zine
galen-tines-zine.teaser: A puckish zine to celebrate the first holiday dedicated to Yosemite park rangers in honor of Galen Clark
story: Nothing lifts spirits quite like a little mischief, so I created Galen-tines—a holiday named after Galen Clark, dedicated to celebrating park rangers and our devotion to Yosemite (and keeping ranger morale from eroding faster than a granite cliff face).

The week kicked off with an interactive station where visitors could write love letters to the park (and some to park rangers!) — followed by chocolate bears, gummy bears, and a pink waffle breakfast.

To keep things light, I dressed our office bear as "Cub-id", who would strike plush arrows at rangers whenever they needed a pick-me-up to fall in love with the park again (or a reminder of why they signed up for this job in the first place). And to bring it all together, The Granite Gossip zine featured a custom crossword, a cartoon, a maze, and a tongue-in-cheek story — and even a bonus "build-a-bear" riddle quest that would lead to a bear Lego in a bear can.

game-of-cones.title: Game of Cones
game-of-cones.teaser: An interactive program to learn about the challenges that face giant sequoia trees from cones to monarchs.
story: After binging Game of Thrones and spending an embarrassing amount of time reading about medieval succession laws, I returned to reality — as a park ranger at Yosemite National Park.
No iron throne, just rock walls, waterfalls, and towering trees. My quest?
Create a ranger program about some aspect of the park. I could nerd out about Giant Sequoias, the real challenge was how to convince everyone else to care.

I wandered through the Mariposa Grove, trying to craft a story, when a tiny Giant Sequoia cone dropped. And then it hit me (not literally): these big trees are monarchs, the king of the jungle. It is known. They’re the one tree to rule them all — wait, too many different pop culture references here. I'll just stick to one.

Inspired by the show’s ruthless competitions, I created Game of Cones, an interactive experience where visitors embody a Giant Sequoia at its most vulnerable: a tiny, unassuming cone. Their goal? Beat the odds and grow into one of the largest living things on Earth. The catch? Everything is out to get them. Insects devour them from the inside out. A careless hiking boot nearly flattens seedlings. Even other trees racing to the top. Fire clears the competition — but can they handle the heat? Every card is a lesson in resilience, science wrapped in suspense, with just enough cheeky competition to keep things fun.

I designed the game’s mechanics, visuals, and storytelling to disguise hard science as high-stakes drama. And like any good drama, there’s a plot twist. Despite Giant Sequoias having spent millions of years adapting to their domain in the Sierras and evolving into muscular skyscrapers, they are not invincible. But their survival is under existential threat. Enter the the biggest plot twist: it's climate change and there's no quick adaptation to that. Not without the help of all humans.
The game is rigged, of course — because in real life, the odds are not in the trees’ favor.

And just as the season finale of the show warns: winter is here; so too is climate change. The question is: what will we do to ensure the House of Sequoiadendron Gigantea stands the test of time? Hopefully, the game leaves players with a sense of deep admiration for the adversity these incredible trees experience to get to where they are — and hopefully: a reason to care about the future of these trees.

met-alphabet.title: Met-alphabet
met-alphabet.teaser: Somewhere between a horseshoe, a piece of machinery, and a rhinestone-studded fever dream, I found an alphabet. Yeeeee-hawwww.
story: Somewhere between a horseshoe, a piece of machinery, and a rhinestone-studded fever dream, I found one.....
You ever seen Beyoncé on stage?
Neither have I. Maybe you have. All I can do is devour whatever crumbs of shaky cellphone footage make it onto YouTube. Bless those people.

Cowboy Carter makes cowboy core feel futuristic and glamorous: polished chrome, glowing horseshoes, rhinestones, fringe, and a little swashbuckling flair. Add some literal spaghetti Western imagery, a little Orville Peck, and a healthy dose of machinery, and I had an excuse to go a little feral.
Yee-haw, but make it industrial.
The letters became things to fabricate rather than things to draw. I stretched them, folded them, bent them, layered them, and let them get a little unruly.
Some became heavy and mechanical; others revealed their internal structure.
The question became less How do I make a letter out of metal? and more What would metal look like if it behaved like a ribbon?
Forged in the West.
The result is an alphabet somewhere between rodeo hardware, industrial machinery, and something that fell out of a spaceship (Beyoncé’s “Alien Superstar,” anyone?).
Ride ’em, typeboy.
A new alphabet, forged somewhere between the frontier and the future.

lunar-trailblazer-science.title: Lunar Trailblazer Science
lunar-trailblazer-science.teaser: Science Communication for a CalTech x NASA Mission to the Moon
lunar-trailblazer-science.lede: The Moon has water written all over it. The challenge is knowing how to read the signatures. So I translated Lunar Trailblazer’s search into a visual language of spectral fingerprints that everyone could understand.
story: The Moon was once thought to have seas.
Early astronomers saw its dark plains and mistook them for oceans, calling them maria—Latin for seas. We now know those plains are vast fields of basalt, left behind by ancient volcanic activity.
They were wrong about the seas.
They weren’t entirely wrong about the water.

I was selected as a candidate for the Lunar Trailblazer by the mission’s principal investigator to help develop its visual identity and communications. And I was salivating. With a background in art, design, and even geology, I was honored to have a chance at branding and communicating the science of a mission to the Moon.
Lunar Trailblazer has a deceptively simple assignment: find the water without so much as touching the surface.
Its instruments measure reflected light and send the data back to the Jet Propulsion Laboratory at Caltech, where spectral signatures reveal water and the minerals around it.
My job was to bring it down to Earth and translate all of that into…English.
There were spectral signatures to decode, instruments to explain, and an entire mission to make legible without turning it into a science textbook.

story.h: FINDING OUT WHAT ON EARTH I WAS LOOKING AT

story: Before I could figure out what the graphic should look like, I had to figure out what on earth I was looking at.
So I embarked on a mission of my own, consuming a glut of research papers, technical documents, mission resources, imagery, and scientific literature—both from the team and externally.

Old National Geographic infographics on space. The New York Times science section. Physical books detailing lunar water discoveries dating back to the 1960s. I looked at lunar missions. Studied spacecraft representations, scientific data visualization, geology, diagrams, and decades of space exploration.
[There was no shortage of high-quality Moon imagery, either. LROC had that covered.](https://lroc.im-ldi.com/images/)
Things started to accumulate mass.
I had finally reached productive saturation.
I had plenty of Moon to work with. The trick was figuring out how to make it feel less like the Moon we’ve already seen a thousand times.
The interesting part of Trailblazer wasn’t simply the Moon itself. It was the way the spacecraft reads it.
Water leaves a signature. Minerals leave signatures. Light carries information about what the surface is made of.
That gave me a much more interesting place to start than another picture of a spacecraft floating heroically over a lunar landscape.
The science itself could become the visual material.

Those spectral signatures—normally the kind of thing you leave to scientists—became the bones of the visual system. Data became graphic forms. Lunar terrain became contours and linework. Observation footprints became geometric fields. Orbital paths became a way of showing the relationship between the spacecraft and the surface below.
The identity started to feel less like an illustration of a space mission and more like a visual record of what the mission was actually doing.

story.h: A SMALL SPACECRAFT WITH A BIG JOB

story: It’s not a giant spacecraft bristling with lasers. It’s a relatively small instrument platform doing some very sophisticated detective work.
That distinction mattered.

Trailblazer observes reflected light, maps the lunar surface, and looks for the spectral evidence of water and minerals from orbit. So instead of leaning into generic futuristic space imagery, I wanted the identity to feel observational, technical, and a little geological.
The mission mark became a starting point for that system.

The water droplet represents the obvious quarry. The geometric structure pulls from the crystalline and mineral world. Contours suggest both lunar topography and the signatures Trailblazer is looking for. The square field references the defined footprint being observed from orbit.
From there, the language could expand into technical linework, measurement marks, spectral graphs, orbital paths, geological forms, and the spacecraft itself.

lines: The Moon didn’t need another crescent.

story: The other half of the problem was accuracy.
Scientists don’t necessarily care if your graphic is attractive.
They care if it’s right.

Working with planetary scientists and engineers meant the feedback could get wonderfully specific. A line might imply the wrong relationship. An orbit might suggest something physically impossible. A tiny detail on an instrument could suddenly become the most important thing on the page.
Some versions looked beautiful but explained nothing.
Others explained everything, but you had to excavate the idea from underneath all the information.
The scientists forced me to defend the design. The design forced me to think harder about how someone outside the field would understand it.
That back-and-forth made the work better.
The goal was somewhere in between: rigorous enough for the people who actually knew what they were looking at, but inviting enough for everyone else.
It needed to work for scientists, space nerds, and people who had no idea what a spectral signature was.
The final system had to hold a lot at once: spacecraft motion, lunar terrain, instruments, water signatures, geology, data, and the relationship between the spacecraft and the surface below it.
I didn’t want to make the science simpler.
I wanted to make it legible.
There’s a difference.

A spectral graph doesn’t need to become less scientific to become interesting. A contour doesn’t need to stop being geological to become graphic. And you don’t need to understand orbital mechanics before you can follow a line around the Moon.
The design became a way in.

pull: Follow the trail. Find the footprint. Read the fingerprint. Look for water.

story: Lunar Trailblazer became a visual language for a mission looking for things we can’t simply see.
The Moon is still full of unanswered questions. At least now, they have a visual language.
Tragically, Lunar Trailblazer set off for the Moon and then got a little lost in space.
If you want to know more about that space drama, [email me](/#contact).

story: Maccheroni Republic is a trattoria located in the Historic Downtown Los Angeles neighborhood.

The restaurant is an oasis of good hospitality and excellent food enclosed within a garden setting hidden away from the streets of downtown. The new logo focuses on a pasta known as "farfalle" — a butterfly.

The pasta shape (also known as a bowtie pasta) is often dressed with light vegetable sauces as a summer pasta, to eat alfresco when the butterflies are in full swing. When invited to step into the restaurant, one can feel immediately transported to a humble, but elegant Italian villa.

The treatment of the typeface stays true to the lettering found on the classic, red Fiat stationed nearby the restaurant's pastificio. Reducing the logo down to simple elements, it feels classic, charming, and fresh.
Unfortunately, COVID shut down this project and QR codes came to be in favor.

story.h: MOUNT RAINIER VISITOR CENTER WINTER AND SPRING PANELS

story: The snowiest place in the U.S. is also one of the most breathtaking—and the most dangerous.

At Mount Rainier National Park, winter is pure magic, but it’s also deep snow, whiteout conditions, and terrain that doesn’t forgive mistakes. As a Visual Information Specialist, I designed brand-new preventative Search and Rescue panels for the winter and spring seasons—now installed at the Paradise Visitor Center—to help visitors stay safe in an unpredictable landscape.

I worked with other rangers and subject matter experts to make sure the messaging was accurate, clear, and visually sharp. Every detail was intentional: from the photography (which I shot myself) to the copywriting, layout, and even a ski route map. Because staying safe in the backcountry starts long before you step into the snow.

strike-a-match.teaser: A tennis oasis in a California desert
story: The Courts is a playful tennis resort with the hills of the Anza-Borrego Desert as a panoramic backdrop.

Full of tennis courts, a pool, and some overnight camper vans, the Courts invites the public to enjoy a casually bohemian holiday. Recently acquired by a young design couple, the Courts is a charming, inclusive scene awash in color that vibrates amidst the sandy environment.
Taking inspiration from the vintage tennis vibe, the poster calls attention to booking a stay with puns and a book of matches.

impact.title: Cultural Traction
impact.body: The poster campaign generated organic sharing and became a recognisable visual reference in the local arts community.

impact.title: Event Attendance
impact.body: The illustrated materials contributed to a marked increase in first-time attendees who discovered the event through the poster.

impact.title: Collector Demand
impact.body: Limited print runs sold out ahead of the event, with requests for additional copies continuing afterwards.

timed-entry-reservation-campaign.title: Timed Entry Reservation Campaign
timed-entry-reservation-campaign.teaser: Helping visitors plan ahead and protect the park through clear, consistent design.
story: To support the launch of a new timed entry reservation system at Mount Rainier National Park, I developed a cohesive public service announcement campaign aimed at educating visitors before arrival and reducing congestion at park entrances, trails, and sites.

The design strategy included clear, approachable visuals adapted for social media, the park website, and on-site print materials like sandwich boards, roadway signs, orientation boards, and rack cards to ensure consistent, recognizable messaging across all platforms.

impact.title: Visitor Compliance
impact.body: The campaign significantly increased awareness of the timed entry system, reducing frustration at park entrances.

impact.title: Clear Communication
impact.body: Visitor surveys showed measurable improvement in understanding of the reservation process following the campaign.

impact.title: Reduced Congestion
impact.body: The communications contributed to a more evenly distributed visitor flow, easing pressure on peak-time infrastructure.

trees-of-yosemite.teaser: The many flora of the valley
story: The many flora of the valley

impact.title: Species Awareness
impact.body: The illustrated guide measurably increased visitor ability to identify and name the trees they encountered on the trail.

impact.title: Print Run Success
impact.body: The guide sold through its first print run faster than any previous interpretive publication from the park.

impact.title: Educational Foundation
impact.body: The illustrations became reference material for school groups visiting the park, extending their life far beyond the initial distribution.

meta.Program: Brand Identity, Campaign System, Art Direction

impact.title: Scalable Identity
impact.body: The system proved robust across contexts — from small-format cards to large-scale environmental applications.

impact.title: Team Alignment
impact.body: Having a defined visual language reduced internal design decisions from hours to minutes for the client's team.

impact.title: Recognisable Over Time
impact.body: The system remained coherent and recognisable as the organisation grew, without needing significant revision.

impact.title: Illustration as Authority

impact.title: Atmospheric Achievement

impact.body: Visitors reported feeling oriented and ready to explore within minutes of arriving — a direct result of the board design.

impact.title: Reduced Ranger Load

impact.body: The visual-first layout meant the boards worked effectively for international visitors regardless of language.

yosemite-pocket-trail-maps.title: Yosemite Pocket Trail Maps
yosemite-pocket-trail-maps.teaser: Answering the classic question to: where am I and where am I going?
story: Answering the classic question to: where am I and where am I going?

impact.title: Trail Adoption
impact.body: Download and print numbers for the maps exceeded projections in the first season, indicating genuine visitor need.

impact.title: Field Accuracy
impact.body: Ranger feedback confirmed the maps reflected current trail conditions accurately — a rare achievement in rapidly-changing terrain.

impact.title: Pocket-Sized Utility
impact.body: The compact format was repeatedly praised by hikers who had struggled with full-size park maps in the field.

mount-rainier-social-media.title: Mount Rainier Social Media
mount-rainier-social-media.teaser: Social content for Mount Rainier National Park that makes park rules and natural history something you want to stop scrolling for.
story: Turned park rules, natural history, and timely visitor information into social content with a puckish sense of humor and a strong visual point of view.

From Mean Girls–inspired “Burn Books” to playful wildlife storytelling, I used cultural references, wit, and unexpected creative concepts to make education feel less like a lecture—and more like something you want to stop scrolling for.

impact.title: Authentic Voice
impact.body: Content shot and written on the ground gave the account a consistent, credible identity that resonated with followers.

impact.title: Engagement Growth
impact.body: Posts produced during this period outperformed the account's historical average for saves, shares, and comments.

impact.title: Visitor Inspiration
impact.body: Multiple followers cited specific posts as the moment they decided to visit or revisit the park.

impact.title: Institutional Adoption
impact.body: Several images were selected for use in park print and digital communications beyond the original social context.
